title: The Hidden Power of Scaling Factor in LoRA Optimization
claim: Scaling factor and learning rate act differently: raising the scale reaches lower loss than tuning the rate, and the optimal scale grows sublinearly with rank.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, line plots with annotation arrow and fit lines
description: Three side-by-side line plots, each with a bold title. (a) Hyperparameter Tuning plots eval loss against learning rate on a log axis. Colored lines are grouped by alpha (red, orange, green, blue) and marker shape shows rank. Gray linear fits run through the minima. A small annotation reads 'α↑ ⇒ η*↓, L*↓'. (b) Scaling Effects plots eval loss against a multiplier relative to the base, on a log axis. Dashed lines vary η and dotted lines vary α, colored by rank from light gray through orange, green and blue. The α paths reach lower minima than the η paths. (c) Relationship Fitting plots optimal α against rank r on log axes. Dark dots lie on a green dashed fit, α≈256√r. A gray dotted line, the conventional α=r, lies far below. The eye goes first to the colorful curves in (a), then to the green fit in (c).
caption: Hyperparameter analysis of Llama 3-1B on the Tulu 3 dataset. (a) Evaluation loss as a function of the learning rate η across different ranks r and scaling factors α. Gray lines denote linear fits of the minimum loss for each (r, α). Increasing α lowers the optimal loss and shifts η∗downward. (b) Scaling paths defined in Eq. (2) relative to the baseline (ηFFT = 2 × 10−5, α0 = 16), where ηFFT denotes the optimal FFT learning rate. Varying α reaches lower-loss regimes that are inaccessible via η-tuning alone. (c) Optimal scaling factor α∗as a function of rank r, evaluated at ηFFT. The observed sublinear trend and large magnitude of α challenge conventional scaling heuristics.
abstract: In Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), the scaling factor $Î±$ is often treated as a mere complement to the learning rate, yet its role in optimization remains poorly understood. In this paper, we reveal that the scaling factor $Î±$ and the learning rate function differently, with $Î±$ emerging as the dominant driver of effective optimization, delivering gains that cannot be replicated by learning rate scaling alone. Through the synergy of extensive empirical analysis and a theoretical Signal-Drift framework, we uncover three findings into LoRA's scaling mechanism: First, LoRA's spectral suppression smooths the optimization landscape, rendering standard hyperparameters overly conservative and creating an optimization gap. Second, when leveraging this smoothness to accelerate convergence, $Î±$ outperforms the learning rate by amplifying the task signal without increasing the drift ratio. Third, the optimal scaling factor follows a sublinear relationship with the rank, well characterized by a square-root law with an unexpectedly large coefficient, revealing the insufficient scaling of existing rank-tied heuristics. Based on these insights, we propose LoRA-$Î±$, a minimalist framework that restores $Î±$ to its principled regime, making LoRA compatible with standard small learning rates. Extensive evaluations across diverse tasks demonstrate that LoRA-$Î±$ consistently improves performance while streamlining hyperparameter search, unleashing the learning potential of LoRA.
